stories.title: Anthropic says Claude designed 17 lab-confirmed protein binders against dangerous scorpion toxins
paragraphs: Anthropic said on Oct. 20 that it asked an internal research model, working inside Claude Science, to design minibinders, small proteins that attach tightly to a target, against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that such binders could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom. The company says the project grew out of a question from the investment research firm Citrini Research about whether AI could let motivated nonexperts tackle a real health problem. Anthropic notes that scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more each year, causing more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in places with limited medical care.

According to Anthropic, the model worked mainly autonomously for 64 hours from an initial prompt plus four follow-ups. It used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 protein designs, screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs and picked 180 designs for testing, and the team added 31 more with Claude's help. The targets were five neurotoxins from scorpions in Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II) and the Middle East (LqhIII). Anthropic says the campaign used on the order of 10,000 GPU hours.

The contract labs Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience tested all 211 designs, and 17 met Anthropic's strict criteria for a binder, each against a single toxin: seven against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I and two against LqhIII. None of the designs aimed at several toxins at once worked against more than one, and Anthropic's X thread says none bound the Brazilian species' toxin. The two strongest, Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, bound Cn2 with affinities in the single-digit nanomolar range, and competition tests suggest they attach at or near the same site as an antibody reported to neutralize Cn2 in mice.

Anthropic stresses that this is exploratory work and that it is not claiming to have produced an antivenom: the binders were tested only against lab-made toxins, not for neutralization in cells or protection in animals. Two outside experts it consulted, Susana Vázquez Torres of Spain's National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO) and Timothy P. Jenkins of the Technical University of Denmark, called it a promising first step. Anthropic is releasing all 211 designs and their lab data on Hugging Face.

stories.title: Japan launches its MMX mission to bring back the first sample from Mars' moon Phobos
paragraphs: Japan's Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched today, Oct. 19, on an H3 rocket from Pad-2 at Tanegashima Space Center's Yoshinobu Launch Complex at 3:41 p.m. EDT, which is 12:41 p.m. PT and 4:41 a.m. on Oct. 20 in Japan, Space.com reports. Space.com says it was the 10th flight of the H3, developed by JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, and that the rocket flew a nominal trajectory over the Pacific, dropping its four solid boosters just before the two-minute mark and its payload fairing about 80 seconds later. According to Space.com, the plan called for the upper stage to fire a second time for a trans-Mars injection burn about one hour and four minutes after liftoff, with MMX released about a minute after that burn ended, roughly 368 miles (592 kilometers) above central Africa. ESA says the mission is led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) together with NASA, the French space agency CNES, the German Aerospace Center DLR and ESA, and it will be the first mission to collect a sample from Phobos and bring it back to Earth.

ESA says MMX will take around a year to reach Mars, entering orbit around the planet in August 2027 and orbiting Phobos from September 2027. After studying Phobos and Deimos from a distance, it is to release the 25-kilogram Idefix rover in early 2029; ESA notes Phobos' gravity is so low that Idefix will weigh the equivalent of 15 grams there. ESA says the main spacecraft will land on Phobos in 2030, and a return module will deliver at least ten grams of Phobos material in a capsule that lands in Australia in 2031. The mission carries 11 science instruments, seven on the main spacecraft and four on the rover, according to ESA. Space.com adds that MMX will spend about three years in the Martian system, making two separate touchdowns on the 14-mile-wide (22 km) Phobos to collect samples and later flying past the smaller moon Deimos several times before leaving for Earth in November 2030.

ESA says the moons may be asteroids captured into Mars orbit or the remnants of debris thrown into orbit by a giant collision on Mars, and that samples are needed to find out. Space.com quotes NASA MMX program executive and program scientist Tom Statler, from an Oct. 15 statement: "Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds." Space.com also reports that MMX was originally supposed to launch in 2024, but problems with the H3 rocket kept it grounded until the next Earth-Mars launch window, which comes once every 26 months.

Science News reports that if MMX succeeds it will be the first mission to reach Phobos, after three earlier Russian spacecraft failed, and that the returned rocks may even contain stray grains blasted off Mars itself. The magazine notes that NASA's plan to fetch the Perseverance rover's samples is in limbo after the U.S. Congress cut funding for that follow-on mission, which has made scientists keen on even an indirect look at Martian material. NASA Johnson Space Center planetary scientist Michael Zolensky told Science News that 15 percent of the sample will eventually go to Johnson, adding, "A few grams of sample are going to be a real bonanza for scientists." Space.com reports that NASA's contributions include the MEGANE gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, a pneumatic sampler built by Honeybee Robotics and Deep Space Network support, about $87 million in total through the end of the mission.

stories.title: Mistral releases Voxtral 3 speech models and a voice agent SDK covering 50+ languages
paragraphs: Mistral AI announced Voxtral 3 on Oct. 20, a new family of speech-to-text and text-to-speech models together with a voice agent SDK that, according to the company, brings listening, reasoning, tool calling and speaking into a single real-time streaming pipeline. Mistral says it is aimed at uses such as contact-center agents, service desks, virtual assistants and hands-free copilots, and is available through its API and for self-deployment on a customer's own infrastructure.

On the listening side, Mistral says Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 is state of the art in multilingual transcription, diarization (identifying who spoke when) and context biasing, where key terms are supplied to improve accuracy, and that it outperforms Whisper, Scribe v2 and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. Supported languages expand to 50, including the 24 official EU languages. The company says the smaller Mini model has 4 billion parameters and costs $0.0035 per minute, and a separate realtime model transcribes at under 500 milliseconds of latency. The models also detect when a speaker has finished talking.

For speech output, Mistral says Voxtral Mini TTS 3 reaches state-of-the-art expressiveness in 35+ languages and 50+ dialects, adjusting emotion, pace and emphasis from the conversation or from tags such as emotion and pacing. A Pro Voice feature can adapt a speaker's voice using up to 30 minutes of recorded audio. Mistral lists the speech model at $13 per million characters and says it costs less to run than comparable models: OpenAI TTS-1, Deepgram, ElevenLabs Flash and Gemini Flash.

The voice agent SDK is built on LiveKit, according to Mistral: a realtime transcription model listens, a general model such as Mistral Small reasons and calls tools, and the speech model replies, with each turn completing in under one second and the agent stopping when the caller interrupts. Mistral says agents can answer and place phone calls over SIP and run in browsers and apps over WebRTC, and that Voxtral 3 is available today through its European, US and global API endpoints.

stories.title: Microplastics aren't chemically inert in water: they spontaneously make reactive hydroxyl radicals, a Nature study reports
paragraphs: Common microplastics are not chemically inert once they are in water, according to a study by researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley, published in the journal Nature on Oct. 14. The paper reports that commodity microplastics spontaneously generate reactive oxygen species, specifically hydroxyl radicals, at the surface where the plastic meets water. ScienceAlert, which covered the study on Oct. 20, describes hydroxyl radicals as among the most reactive and toxic types of free radicals and calls them DNA-damaging.

The team tested six widely used plastics, polypropylene, polyethylene, PVC, polystyrene, PET and PMMA (acrylic), and the paper says it observed spontaneous radical generation for all six. According to the authors, the activity varied from plastic to plastic and increased with how water-repelling, or hydrophobic, the surface is, with polyolefins such as polyethylene and polypropylene showing stronger effects than PET and PMMA. The paper says ab initio calculations support the lab observations and show that oxidizing hydroxide becomes energetically easier at more hydrophobic plastic–water interfaces.

In further lab tests, the researchers report that lysozyme, a protein that ScienceAlert notes is found in tears, saliva, mucus and milk, aggregated on polystyrene microplastics, and that caffeine, used as a radical scavenger, suppressed that aggregation. They also report that some mouse red blood cells exposed to polystyrene microplastics developed fragmented, helmet-like shapes. The authors write that their findings challenge the prevailing view that plastics are inert and identify a possibly overlooked mechanism for the harmful effects of microplastics on health and the environment.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate [these] high-energy reactive radicals," first author Naixin Qian of Columbia University said, as quoted by ScienceAlert. Berkeley theoretical chemist Teresa Head-Gordon said the work "could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment." ScienceAlert reports that co-authors are now using animal studies to look at how plastic particles migrate into fetal tissue during gestation. The Nature paper is open access.

stories.title: Mathematicians say an OpenAI proof of the 'quasi-Riemann hypothesis' looks correct, calling its implications 'staggering'
paragraphs: Number theorists who have spent the past two weeks studying an AI-generated proof released by OpenAI on Oct. 6 largely agree that it is correct, Quanta Magazine reported on Oct. 19. The proof claims to settle the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, which has been open for more than 160 years and concerns how prime numbers are distributed. Jared Duker Lichtman of Stanford University called it "the most significant AI-for-math achievement so far, by quite a margin," and Maksym Radziwiłł of New York University told Quanta the implications are "staggering," adding that "the vast majority of consequences of RH already follow from quasi-RH."

Quanta explains that the Riemann hypothesis says all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have a real part of 1/2, while the quasi version only asks for proof that they lie in a vertical strip narrower than the known one between 0 and 1. According to Quanta, OpenAI announced two versions: one dated Sept. 30, 199 pages long and formally verified in the Lean programming language, placing the zeros between 1/8 and 7/8, and a 49-page version completed almost a week later, not yet formally verified, placing them between 1/12 and 11/12. Mathematicians have focused on the shorter paper, which Quanta says is the only one of OpenAI's Oct. 6 papers to have been edited by a person; OpenAI told the magazine, "The paper is the result of work from everyone at OpenAI."

Radziwiłł told Quanta that both papers are "horribly written," falling well short of the field's standards of clarity, but that he can now sketch the argument in half a page. Experts quoted by the magazine say the proof introduces no new concepts and instead combines long-known ideas, including obscure objects called metaplectic forms and a formula that Radziwiłł and Alexander Dunn of the Georgia Institute of Technology proved in 2021. Quanta reports that Princeton's Peter Sarnak has repurposed a course he is teaching this semester to study the proof, and that he said he won't be satisfied it is "a Theorem" until humans check and understand all the details.

According to Quanta, mathematicians expect the result to establish many other results in number theory, geometry and theoretical computer science, but they are skeptical that the same techniques can reach the full Riemann hypothesis. "It seems most likely to me that once mathematicians have fully internalized the new methods and worked through their implications, we will still feel as far off from the full Riemann hypothesis as we were before," Will Sawin of Princeton told the magazine, adding, "But I am not certain of this."

stories.title: DeepSeek open-sources DeepInfer, the inference framework behind its DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash service
paragraphs: Chinese AI lab DeepSeek has released DeepInfer, which it calls its in-house inference framework, as fully open source, the company announced on X on Oct. 20. According to DeepSeek, the software powers DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at scale with high throughput and low latency, and the company says it is sharing its production stack to help the community lower compute costs, reduce energy use and make AI more affordable.

The project's GitHub page describes DeepInfer as the high-performance inference framework that powers DeepSeek's large-scale production services and says this release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale. It lists DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the supported model, and NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs as the supported hardware. The code is released under the Apache License 2.0.

Listed features include optimized kernels built on DeepSeek's own open-source libraries such as FlashMLA, DeepGEMM and DeepEP, data parallelism for attention and expert parallelism for its mixture-of-experts layers, faster decoding with draft tokens and confidence-scheduled verification, asynchronous batch scheduling, batch-invariant inference, deterministic sampling, and structured outputs that constrain generation to a regex, JSON schema or grammar. DeepSeek's X thread says inference code for future DeepSeek models and ongoing optimizations will land in the same project.

The README notes that some parts of a complete inference service are not included in this release: a KV cache system, separation of the prefill and decode stages across machines, and load balancing across data-parallel replicas. It says its published performance benchmarks were measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode, and that DeepInfer was originally built primarily on the open-source vLLM project, with additional inspiration from SGLang and NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM.
